_meta: A record containing special floating-point values (NaN and infinity) alongside an ordinary number, used to show that JSON has no way to represent NaN or infinity and that Python's json encoder, by default, emits them anyway as the bare tokens NaN, Infinity, and -Infinity -- producing text that Python can read back but that strict JSON parsers in other languages reject. The JSON specification defines numbers as ordinary decimals; there is no NaN, no Infinity, no -Infinity in the grammar. Yet floating-point computations produce these values constantly: 0.0/0.0 gives NaN, a sum that overflows gives infinity, a missing measurement is often stored as NaN. When such a value reaches json.dumps, Python's default (allow_nan=True) writes the bare word NaN or Infinity into the output -- a non-standard extension. The result is text that json.loads (equally lenient) will happily parse back, so the data round-trips within Python and the bug stays hidden; but the moment the same text is sent to JavaScript's JSON.parse, or a strict parser in another language or service, it is rejected as malformed, because those tokens are not valid JSON. The fixes are to pass allow_nan=False so json.dumps raises at serialization time (catching the value early), or to sanitize the special values to null (or a documented sentinel) before dumping. record maps field names to values; some are the special floats, described here since JSON itself cannot store them. The Python object is rebuilt in code; the default (non-standard) serialization, its rejection by a strict parser, and the sanitized valid serialization are computed.
record_values_note: ok=1.0 (normal), ratio=NaN (0/0), score=Infinity (overflow); NaN and Infinity cannot be written in this JSON fixture, so the code constructs them
